opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favorite examples, because it's almost exactly the experiment we used to do with patients in the hospital.

When I was working with epilepsy patients who had electrodes implanted in their brains, we could record from individual neurons. You'd find a cell that fires when the person sees a specific concept, say a particular actor, or the Eiffel Tower. Then you'd ask them to just *think* about that thing, with nothing on the screen, and the same neuron would light up. The thought and the perception share the same machinery. Imagining is, in a sense, replaying.

What people at Anthropic and other labs have started to do with models like Claude is conceptually very similar. They look inside the network and find directions or "features" that correspond to a concept. There's a pattern of activity that means "elephant." When you show it a sentence about elephants, that pattern activates. When you tell it to think about elephants without writing about them, you can still see the elephant representation turn on internally, even though the output says nothing about elephants. And if you tell it *not* to think about elephants, it often still activates a little, which is the classic "don't think of a pink elephant" problem we have as humans. The instruction to suppress something requires you to represent it.

So the resemblance is real at the functional level. Both systems seem to have an internal representation of a concept that is separate from saying the concept out loud. There's a gap between what's going on inside and what comes out, and you can measure that gap. For me, as someone who spent years trying to read thoughts from neurons, that's fascinating, because with the model you can do things we could never ethically do in a human. You can turn the elephant feature up and watch the model start talking about elephants everywhere. You can turn it down and see what breaks.

But I'd be careful about the leap from "it has a representation that behaves like ours" to "it's like a brain" in every sense. The architecture is very different. A brain is wet, noisy, embodied, it has hormones and a body and a history of survival behind it. Claude is a mathematical object trained on text. What I think the elephant example shows is that some principles of how you represent information might be general. If you're any system trying to model the world efficiently, you might end up with something like a concept cell, whether you're made of neurons or of matrices.

And honestly, that's the part that keeps me up at night in a good way. If we find the same solutions in silicon that evolution found in biology, it tells us those solutions aren't accidents of being human. They might be something closer to the laws of how minds, any minds, have to work.

fable-5.1.text:
So here's what's beautiful about it. When Anthropic's interpretability team looked inside Claude, they found that when you prompt it with elephants, there's a specific cluster of activity, a feature, that lights up for "elephant," and it fires not just for the word but for the concept. It fires if you describe a big grey animal with a trunk. It fires in French. It fires for a picture of an elephant. And that's exactly what we see in the human brain.

I spent years recording from single neurons in patients with epilepsy, and we found cells, famously the so-called "Jennifer Aniston neuron," that respond to a person whether you show them a photo, or the name written out, or you say the name aloud. The neuron doesn't care about the modality. It cares about the concept. And here's the other piece: if you tell someone "don't think of an elephant," that neuron fires anyway. You can't suppress it. The thought is already there before the instruction to not think arrives. And Claude does something very similar. You tell it not to mention elephants and the elephant feature still activates internally, it just suppresses the output.

Now, I want to be careful. Nobody designed Claude to mimic the brain. These are completely different substrates, silicon versus wet carbon, trained in completely different ways. So when two systems that were built differently converge on the same solution, that tells you something about the problem itself. Maybe there's only a small number of efficient ways to represent a concept like "elephant," and both evolution and gradient descent stumbled into one of them.

What I find most interesting, honestly, is that we now have a second brain to study that we can fully open up. In neuroscience I get to listen to maybe a hundred neurons at a time, in a patient, in a hospital, for a few days. With Claude you can look at everything, freeze it, rerun it, poke at a single feature and see what changes. It's the experiment I always wanted to run on humans and never could. So I think of it less as "AI is like the brain" and more as: we finally have a model organism for thought.

astra-6.text:
The resemblance is that thinking about an elephant involves a pattern of activity, rather than one place that contains the whole idea of an elephant. In a human brain, that might involve associations with its shape, its size, a memory of seeing one. With Claude, the interesting question is whether there are internal patterns that reliably correspond to that concept, even when you change the wording of the prompt.

If there are, that suggests a similarity in how information is represented. But we have to separate that from the claim that Claude experiences an elephant the way you do. A similar pattern of computation doesn’t, by itself, establish a similar subjective experience.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s interesting is that you can look inside the model and find patterns of activity associated with the concept of an elephant. It’s not necessarily one little place where “elephant” lives; it’s a pattern across many components. And that resembles something we see in the brain: thinking about something can reactivate some of the machinery involved in recognizing it.

But we have to be careful about what that resemblance tells us. It doesn’t mean Claude pictures an elephant the way you do, or that it has a subjective experience of one. It means that two very different systems may have arrived at some similar ways of organizing information. That makes these models interesting tools for asking questions about the brain, even when the answers turn out to be different.
